We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

Illuminating Krzysztof Szczawinski 🇵🇱 (@Kristof_Poland) Now the Third Man – Rudi Dutschke – The Man Who Gave the Long March Its Name. Gramsci invented the strategy. Dutschke named it – and then went out and implemented it, in the streets of West Berlin, in 1968, with a generation of students who had read Gramsci and were ready to march. 1. Born in East Germany in 1940, he fled to West Berlin in 1961 – two days before the Wall went up. He had seen actually existing socialism from the inside – and concluded not that the project was wrong, but that the method was. He didn’t want that version. He wanted a better one – built from the inside of the Western institutions rather than imposed from above by a party apparatus. 2. He read Gramsci. He read Mao. And he synthesized them into the phrase that named the entire project: der lange Marsch durch die Institutionen – the long march through the institutions. Not Gramsci’s phrase. Dutschke’s. Gramsci had described the mechanism. Dutschke gave it the slogan that made it actionable, transmissible, and operational for an entire generation. The phrase spread across Europe in 1968 like a match dropped in dry grass. Every student who heard it understood immediately what it meant and what it required. 3. The target was precisely identified: not the state, not the economy, but the institutions that reproduced the cultural hegemony – the universities, the media, the schools, the churches, the legal system. Infiltrate them. Occupy them from within. Replace the people who ran them with people who shared the counter-hegemonic project. Don’t storm the Reichstag. Get a job in the editorial office. Get a position in the faculty. Get appointed to the curriculum committee. The revolution would happen through tenure, not through barricades. 4. On April 11, 1968, Josef Bachmann shot Dutschke in the head on the Kurfürstendamm in West Berlin. Three bullets. Dutschke survived – but never fully recovered. He spent the rest of his life in partial recovery, moving between Germany, Denmark, and Britain, still writing, still thinking, still speaking at conferences with the damaged brain of a man who had been shot for his ideas. He died in 1979, drowning in his bathtub during an epileptic seizure caused by the brain damage from the shooting. He was thirty-nine. 5. The shooting produced something Bachmann had not intended: it made Dutschke a martyr and the movement a cause. The protests that followed — directed primarily at the Axel Springer media company, whose tabloid Bild the students blamed for inciting violence — were the largest street demonstrations in West Germany since the war. The attempt to silence the long march accelerated it. The generation radicalized by the shooting went on to become exactly what Dutschke had described: the professors, the journalists, the civil servants, the judges. The bullet proved his point. 6. Gramsci designed the theory in a prison in Italy. Dutschke gave it its name and its generation in Berlin. The 1968 student movement he led was the transmission mechanism – the moment the Prison Notebooks left the academy and became a political program with a slogan, a street presence, and a generational identity. Without Dutschke, Gramsci remains a text. With Dutschke, he becomes a movement. The long march through the institutions began, as a practical matter, in West Berlin in 1968, among students who knew precisely where they were going and had a name for the route. 7. The institutions they marched through are now theirs. The universities, the media, the civil service, the judiciary – all transformed, over fifty years, exactly as Dutschke described. He was shot for saying it could be done. It was done. The man who named the march did not live to see its completion. He died at thirty-nine in a bathtub, from the damage done by a bullet fired by someone who thought killing him would stop the march. It did not stop the march. It never does. Ideas shot in the head have a way of surviving their authors. Even the bad ones. — http://nitter.jaydenha.uk/Kristof_Poland/status/2096588222373515719#m

OpenWorker -- an open source agent that doesn't just chat but completes tasks on your laptop -- just released a new version with many features for security workflows. After our initial release, many users found it especially useful for cybersecurity. Attackers are already using AI; OpenWorker is committed to giving defenders the same leverage. Running an agent requires both (i) A model and (ii) A harness (the software around the model). Because the OpenWorker harness is fully open source, security teams can audit it to make sure we haven't built any backdoors that exfiltrate your code and data to some company or even a foreign adversary. OpenWorker now comes with built-in cybersecurity agents for (i) Scanning your code for vulnerabilities. (ii) Scanning dependencies for supply chain injections. (iii) Checking your cloud security configuration for attack surfaces. This enables developers to do much more security work before deployment (part of what's called the "shift left" movement). You choose the model: you can run open weight models fully locally so sensitive code never leaves your machine. This helps with legitimate security work (like reproducing a known exploit to defend against it) that can trigger refusals in leading closed models. Or use your ChatGPT subscription, or stealth preview models like Ox Alpha, or any model via API key. Thanks also to all the open source contributors! tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une bonne longue session de divagations. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime me détendre, passer en mode /voice et simplement divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, tout y passe, un flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare au début, quelque chose comme 'je passe en reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe...'. Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont en quelque sorte très bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de votre propre enchevêtrement de pensées ressort beaucoup plus propre que ce que vous aviez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la fusion mentale et avez moins de choses à corriger à partir de ce moment-là.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

idees.text_fr: Nous commençons à quitter le territoire où l'on testerait un grand modèle de langage (LLM) en lui demandant par exemple de 'créer un SVG d'un pélican à bicyclette'. Pour généraliser l'idée, j'étais curieux de voir ce qu'Opus 5 ferait si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1 million de tokens (environ 10$) et que je lui demandais un rendu 3D en JS. Opus a travaillé pendant environ 2 heures et a écrit 5500 lignes de code qui ont rendu (de manière procédurale) l'histoire. C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais il est assez stupéfiant qu'un LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux en coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire le code qui anime tout cela, et qu'il fasse même quoi que ce soit. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples parce que personne de sensé ne passerait jamais le temps d'écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, c'est donc un exemple où l'on passe de 'personne ne ferait jamais ça' à 'bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est presque gratuit'. Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé à l'idée de créer des mondes hyper-personnalisés dans lesquels on pourrait imaginer plonger des joueurs, par exemple ici pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère de X à la demande. Une dernière pensée est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLM : ils ne peuvent pas facilement vérifier leur travail car ils ne sont pas capables de percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou de jouer à des jeux à l'intérieur d'eux. Ici, Opus 5 a dû prendre des captures d'écran très lentement et minutieusement à différents moments, et il a fait quelques erreurs et créé pas mal de désordre. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, fait encore pas mal défaut. Vidéo
idees.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

outils.text_fr: OpenWorker – un agent open source qui ne se contente pas de discuter mais qui accomplit des tâches sur votre ordinateur portable – vient de publier une nouvelle version avec de nombreuses fonctionnalités pour les flux de travail de sécurité. Après notre première publication, de nombreux utilisateurs l'ont trouvé particulièrement utile pour la cybersécurité. Les attaquants utilisent déjà l'IA ; OpenWorker s'engage à donner aux défenseurs le même avantage. L'exécution d'un agent nécessite à la fois (i) un modèle et (ii) un harnais (le logiciel autour du modèle). Parce que le harnais d'OpenWorker est entièrement open source, les équipes de sécurité peuvent l'auditer pour s'assurer que nous n'avons pas construit de portes dérobées qui exfiltrent votre code et vos données vers une entreprise ou même un adversaire étranger. OpenWorker est désormais livré avec des agents de cybersécurité intégrés pour (i) analyser votre code à la recherche de vulnérabilités. (ii) analyser les dépendances pour les injections dans la chaîne d'approvisionnement. (iii) vérifier votre configuration de sécurité cloud pour les surfaces d'attaque. Cela permet aux développeurs de faire beaucoup plus de travail de sécurité avant le déploiement (une partie de ce qu'on appelle le mouvement 'shift left'). Vous choisissez le modèle : vous pouvez exécuter des modèles à poids ouverts entièrement localement afin que le code sensible ne quitte jamais votre machine. Cela aide avec le travail de sécurité légitime (comme reproduire un exploit connu pour s'en défendre) qui peut déclencher des refus dans les principaux modèles fermés. Ou utilisez votre abonnement ChatGPT, ou des modèles d'aperçu furtif comme Ox Alpha, ou n'importe quel modèle via une clé API. Merci également à tous les contributeurs open source ! Rejoignez le travail avec @rohitcprasad alors suivez-le aussi pour obtenir des mises à jour plus fréquentes. Essayez-le : openworker.com/ Code : github.com/andrewyng/openwor…
outils.text_original: OpenWorker -- an open source agent that doesn't just chat but completes tasks on your laptop -- just released a new version with many features for security workflows. After our initial release, many users found it especially useful for cybersecurity. Attackers are already using AI; OpenWorker is committed to giving defenders the same leverage. Running an agent requires both (i) A model and (ii) A harness (the software around the model). Because the OpenWorker harness is fully open source, security teams can audit it to make sure we haven't built any backdoors that exfiltrate your code and data to some company or even a foreign adversary. OpenWorker now comes with built-in cybersecurity agents for (i) Scanning your code for vulnerabilities. (ii) Scanning dependencies for supply chain injections. (iii) Checking your cloud security configuration for attack surfaces. This enables developers to do much more security work before deployment (part of what's called the "shift left" movement). You choose the model: you can run open weight models fully locally so sensitive code never leaves your machine. This helps with legitimate security work (like reproducing a known exploit to defend against it) that can trigger refusals in leading closed models. Or use your ChatGPT subscription, or stealth preview models like Ox Alpha, or any model via API key. Thanks also to all the open source contributors! Join work with @rohitcprasad so please follow him too to get more frequent updates. Try it out: openworker.com/ Code: github.com/andrewyng/openwor…
outils.decryptage: Un projet 'open source' signifie que son code est accessible à tous, permettant la transparence et la contribution. Une 'porte dérobée' (backdoor) est un moyen caché d'accéder à un système, souvent à des fins malveillantes.

outils.text_fr: Mistral OCR 4 a transformé un examen de calcul manuscrit en LaTeX propre ! Nous lui avons donné une photo d'une page d'examen manuscrite. Le modèle a lu l'écriture et a reconstruit chaque formule en texte numérique structuré. Sortie : Temps : 5,1s · Coût : 0,09$. Les formules étaient exactement correctes – la partie difficile a été réussie. Le graphique, malheureusement, n'a pas été redessiné. Mais c'est la partie révélatrice : la plupart des outils OCR se contentent de vider le texte et de laisser tomber la figure discrètement. OCR 4 a détecté le tracé, l'a encadré et l'a étiqueté comme un graphique. Il n'est pas redessiné, mais il est lu et pris en compte. Vidéo Mistral AI (@MistralAI) Présentation de Mistral OCR 4. Il crée une structure avec des cadres de délimitation, une classification par blocs et des scores de confiance en ligne dans 170 langues. 🧵👇 — http://nitter.jaydenha.uk/MistralAI/status/2069420263825895917#m
outils.text_original: Mistral OCR 4 turned a handwritten calculus exam into clean LaTeX! We gave it a photo of a hand-written exam page. The model read the handwriting and rebuilt every formula into structured digital text Output: Time: 5.1s · Cost: $0.09 Formulas came through exactly right - the hard part was nailed. The graph, unfortunately, it didn’t redraw. But that’s the telling part: most OCR tools just dump the text and quietly drop the figure. OCR 4 caught the plot, boxed it, and tagged it as a chart. It doesn’t get redrawn, but it gets read and accounted for Video Mistral AI (@MistralAI) Introducing Mistral OCR 4. It creates structure with bounding boxes, block classification, and inline confidence scores in 170 languages. 🧵👇 — http://nitter.jaydenha.uk/MistralAI/status/2069420263825895917#m
outils.decryptage: L'OCR (Reconnaissance Optique de Caractères) est une technologie qui permet de convertir différents types de documents (comme des images numérisées) en données textuelles modifiables. LaTeX est un système de composition de documents largement utilisé pour les écrits scientifiques et techniques.
